Regarding the phrase "the day of eternity", al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as the day on which eternity is decreed, whereas others take it as an unending duration. The promise that they will have whatever they wish is understood as the fulfilment of everything souls desire and eyes delight in. The "increase" (mazid) receives several interpretations: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, through several chains, that it is gazing upon the face of God; others see it as the multiplication of good deeds; al-Mawardi relates it to the dark-eyed spouses; and al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur understand it as a favour no one has imagined. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite hadiths about the day of Friday, but Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the precise form of this increase remains unspecified.

This passage describes how the people of the Garden will be told to enter in peace, safe from grief, anger, punishment, and every hardship they suffered in the world; this is the day of eternity, when there is no death and no departure. The commentators explain that they will have whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in, and that with God there is a further increase beyond what they could imagine. Most agree that this increase is a bounty the mind cannot grasp, in line with the authentic hadith: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen.' They differ on its specific nature. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, relying on reports, take it to be gazing upon God's face, while al-Mawardi and others mention the multiplication of good deeds or the maidens of paradise, and al-Shawkani and al-Alusi relate a report of clouds raining down whatever the people desire. Regarding the Fire, which asks whether there is more, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the question is literal and supported by hadith, while others read it figuratively. On the phrase 'they roamed the lands', al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain it as traversing the earth in search of escape from death, and the reading with a kasra attested from Yahya ibn Ya'mur is taken as a warning.

God tells us that before the Quraysh He destroyed generations that were stronger than them in might, and that these peoples travelled and roamed the lands in search of a way to escape destruction, yet found no refuge from God's command. The commentators agree that qarn means a generation of people and that tanqib means roaming and travelling through the land. Ibn Abbas understood it as leaving traces upon the land, al-Hasan as ruling over it, while Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir took it to mean travelling in search of livelihood or escape; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others cite a line of Imru' al-Qays in support. As for mahis, Ibn Zayd explained it as a means of escaping death and Qatada as a way out from God's command. Most readers take fanaqqabu as a past-tense report about those peoples, while Yahya ibn Ya'mur read it as an imperative, a threat addressed to the Meccans; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the subject may also be the Meccans themselves, travelling among the ancient peoples. The following verses are read by the commentators as a reminder for whoever has an understanding heart or who listens attentively while present in mind; Mujahid and Ibn Kathir took 'heart' to mean intellect, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understood it as a living, aware heart.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the mention of earlier peoples, stronger than the Quraysh, who were destroyed and found no escape from God's command. Their destruction is a reminder and an admonition. For most, "heart" means the understanding intellect, since the heart is its seat; Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to be the living heart that grasps what it hears, and al-Shibli a heart present with God. As for "gives ear", most take it to mean listening attentively with the mind present, since whoever is not mentally present is as though absent. On "and he is a witness", most understand presence and alertness of mind, while Qatada reads it as bearing witness to the truth of what is in the scriptures; Hasan and others say the verse refers to Jews and Christians, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Salih take it to mean the people of the Quran. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur favour the sense of presence and attentiveness. Al-Razi notes that "or" distinguishes between the one who understands by himself and the one who needs to be taught. Commentators also connect the passage to the call to patience, prayer and remembrance of God in the face of the disbelievers' words.

This verse states that God created the heavens, the earth and everything between them in six days, and that He was not afflicted by any weariness in doing so. The commentators agree that the denial of fatigue responds to the Jews who claimed that God finished the creation in six days and then rested on the Sabbath. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse was revealed in this context, and one tradition links it to a question the Jews put to the Prophet about the details of creation. Several exegetes, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, draw from it an argument for resurrection: whoever created the heavens and the earth without being worn out can all the more easily bring the dead back to life. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse follows passages describing the creation of the sky and the earth, and that it answers those who denied resurrection. Al-Razi holds that the word 'days' refers to stages or periods rather than days in the ordinary sense, while others take it literally. Al-Shinqiti explains that lughub means the exhaustion that follows labour, so denying the greater implies denying the lesser. All agree that the verse offers consolation to the Prophet and affirms God's power in creation and resurrection.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with what his opponents say, and to glorify his Lord with praise. The commentators agree that this glorification includes prayer. As for the two times, before sunrise and before sunset, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that they refer to the dawn and afternoon prayers, while Ibn Abbas says they mean the noon and afternoon prayers, a view also taken by al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi. Regarding part of the night, Mujahid understands the night prayer at any hour, Ibn Zayd the evening prayer of isha, and Ibn Juzayy the maghrib and isha prayers. As for the hours after prostration, most authorities, including Umar, Ali, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan, take them to be the two units after maghrib, whereas Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd speak of voluntary prayers after the obligatory ones, and Abu al-Ahwas of dhikr after prayers. Al-Tabari prefers the two units after maghrib because of the scholarly consensus. Several commentators link the passage to a reply to Jews who claimed God rested on the Sabbath, and some hold that the command to patience was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to bear patiently what his opponents say and to glorify his Lord, praising Him, at specific times. Most commentators understand the glorification (tasbih) to mean prayer. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and the majority say that glorifying before sunrise means the dawn prayer and glorifying before sunset means the afternoon prayer, as Jarir ibn Abd Allah reports in a hadith about seeing God. Ibn Abbas, in another report, includes the midday prayer. For "part of the night", Ibn Zayd takes it to be the night prayer, Muqatil the sunset and night prayers together, and Mujahid the night prayer at any hour.

The phrase "adbar al-sujud" (the backs of the prostrations) is the most debated. Umar, Ali, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Awza'i take it to mean the two units of prayer after maghrib, relying on reports traced to Ali and Ibn Abbas. Ibn Zayd understands the voluntary prayers after the obligatory ones, Ibn Abbas at one point the witr after isha, and Abu al-Ahwas the glorifications recited after prayers, which Ibn al-Arabi considers the strongest view on reflection. Al-Tabari favours the two units after maghrib because the scholars agree on it, though he says that without that consensus he would have preferred Ibn Zayd's view, since God did not limit the phrase to one prayer.

On recitation, Nafi, Ibn Kathir and Hamza read "idbar" with a kasra, a verbal noun meaning the ending of the prostration, while the others read "adbar" with a fatha as the plural of "dubur". Al-Tabari prefers the latter reading.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to listen for the day when the caller will call from a nearby place. Most commentators identify the caller as Israfil, who will blow the trumpet to summon the dead to gather for judgment. Several report, through Qatada and Ka'b, that the call will come from the rock of Jerusalem, which they describe as the closest point of earth to heaven and the centre of the earth, though the stated distances differ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relay these reports without settling their details. Ibn Jurayj and al-Qurtubi, citing Ikrima, explain instead that nearness means everyone hears the call alike.

The commentators agree that the cry is the cry of resurrection, which is taken to be the true resurrection beyond doubt, and that this day is the day of coming forth from the graves. They differ on the sense of the command to listen. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take it to mean wait, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as attending to what is being revealed about the terrors of the Last Day.

The context is one of consolation for the Prophet and warning to his opponents. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that God knows what they say and that the Prophet was not sent to compel them to believe. Mujahid and al-Kalbi take this to mean he has no power to force them, whereas Qatada reads it as a prohibition against tyranny. Most agree that the Qur'an is to remind only those who fear God's warning.

This passage describes the Day of Resurrection, when the Prophet ﷺ is told to listen for the caller on the day people are raised. The commentators explain that the Cry is the second blast of the trumpet, which all creatures will hear in truth, meaning the resurrection that is beyond doubt, and that this day is the day of coming out from the graves. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, identify the caller as Israfil. The nearby place is taken by al-Tabari and others to be the rock of Jerusalem, said by Ka'b to be eighteen miles from the sky, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see its nearness as meaning that all hear it equally. Ibn al-Jawzi places the call at the gathering place. Al-Mawardi gives two readings of "with the truth": the true word, or the resurrection itself. Al-Razi lists several ways of parsing the verse and of understanding the Cry. On the meaning of listening, Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as waiting, while most take it as paying attention to the account of the events of the end. The commentators agree that the following verses console the Prophet ﷺ. The phrase "you are not a tyrant over them" does not mean compelling faith; al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi regard it as abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas Ibn Kathir reads it as meaning he is only a messenger. The passage ends with the command to remind, through the Qur'an, those who fear the threat.

The verse states that God alone gives life and causes death, and that all creatures will ultimately return to Him. The commentators read the following verses as describing that return: on the day the earth splits open, people will come out of their graves quickly, and gathering them is easy for God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di explain this as the resurrection, while al-Sam'ani and al-Nasafi keep to the plain sense of returning to God for judgment. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya explain the grammar: the word quickly describes those coming out, and al-Tabari links the day to the word return.

All agree that the power to give life and death belongs to God alone, and Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi stress that no one shares it with Him. Al-Qasimi reads life as the light of life being poured out or cut off. Al-Biqa'i sees the repeated divine pronoun as a strong affirmation of the resurrection that the disbelievers denied, and al-Shawkani and al-Sha'rawi say much the same.

Ibn Kathir gives a detailed account: God sends a rain that makes bodies grow in the graves as seeds grow in the soil, then the souls return to the bodies and the earth splits. He cites a hadith in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet will be the first from whom the earth splits. Al-Qurtubi mentions the caller and the trumpet.

Ibn Ashur offers a different reading. Linking the verse to the context of warning, he suggests that the day of coming out may refer to the battle of Badr, when the Quraysh hurried out after a call for help. However, most commentators understand this day as the Last Day.

This verse states that God gives life and causes death, and that all will return to Him. On the day the earth splits open and the dead emerge, they will come out hastening, and this gathering for judgement is easy for God. The commentators agree on the plain sense: people rise from their graves and hurry toward the place of reckoning. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir describe how the earth splits after a rain that makes bodies grow, as seeds sprout in soil, and how an angel then blows the trumpet; Ibn Kathir relays these details without objection, while other commentators do not mention them. The word "hastening" is read in different ways: al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi take it as describing those who come out, whereas Abu Hayyan notes two grammatical readings, one attaching it to the pronoun "them" and the other to an implied verb of going out. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Alusi argue that placing "upon Us" before "easy" signals exclusivity: only the Almighty, whom no affair distracts, can do such a thing. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see the verse as a reply to those who denied resurrection. Most identify the crier as Israfil, while others name Jibril, and several place his call on the rock of Jerusalem, with distance figures that al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi report without deciding. The variant readings of the verb differ only in the doubling of a consonant, with little effect on the meaning.

In this verse God tells His Prophet that He knows best what the disbelievers say, and that he has no power to compel them to believe. His duty is to remind those who fear God's threat through the Quran. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and most commentators read the word jabbar as one who dominates and forces, so the Prophet was not sent to compel them to Islam but to warn and convey the message. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it as a prohibition of arrogance toward them. Al-Tabari supports the sense of compulsion, citing al-Farra and al-Kalbi, who explain that the word comes from jabarahu, meaning he forced him. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya also mention other senses, such as lord or tyrant. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as both a consolation to the Prophet and a threat to the disbelievers, and mentions the possibility of forbearance and gentleness toward them. Several commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Shawkani, hold that the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, while Ibn Ashur rejects this and sees the verse as clarifying the Prophet's role as a caller and guide, not a compeller. All agree that the reminder benefits only the one who fears the threat. A report from Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says that the believers asked the Prophet to warn them more strongly, and this is the occasion given for the verse.
